descripcion: At B1 you place adverbs of frequency, like always, usually and never, correctly: before the main verb but after the verb be. This basic word-order rule prevents one of the most common and noticeable mistakes at this level.

ejemplos.texto: She always arrives exactly on time.
She is always on time for meetings.
I usually have coffee in the morning.

notas: With a normal verb, the frequency adverb goes before it: she always arrives.
With be, the adverb goes after it: she is always.
Never makes the sentence negative in meaning without needing not: I never go there.

contraste.es: Spanish places frequency adverbs more freely, often at the start of the sentence (siempre llega a tiempo). Spanish speakers tend to put always at the start of the English sentence, where it sounds unnatural.
contraste.de: German places frequency adverbs after the verb (Er kommt immer pünktlich), which leads to He comes always on time. German also puts time before place (Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin), while English usually puts place before time: I'm going to Berlin tomorrow.
contraste.it: Italian places frequency and manner adverbs after the verb (arriva sempre in orario; parlo bene l'inglese), which leads to He arrives always on time and I speak well English.
contraste.fr: French places frequency adverbs after the verb (il arrive toujours à l'heure), which leads to He arrives always on time. In compound tenses, however, French puts the adverb between the auxiliary and the participle (il a souvent voyagé), exactly like English (he has often travelled).
contraste.pt: Brazilian Portuguese places sempre before the verb (ele sempre chega na hora), which matches English (He always arrives on time). European Portuguese places it after the verb (chega sempre a horas), which leads to He arrives always on time.

errores: Placing the frequency adverb at the start of the sentence.
Putting the adverb before be instead of after it.
Using not together with never, which is redundant.
autochequeo: Is the frequency adverb before the main verb?
Is it after be, not before?
Have I avoided using not together with never?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the position of frequency adverbs relative to be and to main verbs. Check whether the sentence sounds natural rather than translated. Do not rewrite the text.
